rationale: B wins because it turns the same facts into reporter-ready decision points instead of dressing the relaunch up as a trend before the evidence exists. A's weakest kept angle, "AI matchmaking just went mainstream," overclaims from one Bumble relaunch, then quietly admits it needs proof from other dating apps. B's "Whether a redesign can reverse a paying-user decline is now a public test" is cleaner: it makes the missing post-relaunch user data the story instead of pretending the turnaround has happened.
gaps_in_A: "AI matchmaking just went mainstream" is an overclaim. One Bumble relaunch does not prove mainstream adoption or a category-standard feature.
"her first fix is AI" and "first major public move back in the seat" are not supplied facts. Maybe true, maybe not; a reporter will not let that slide.
"the company's public answer to the falling stock price and user decline" assigns motive that the update does not prove. Frame it as a bet, not as Bumble's stated answer.
The next step jumps to `find-journalists` too soon. The set still needs citable user criticism, exact decline figures, and current coverage checks before anyone starts building a list.
gaps_in_B: "first substantive product move since the founder's return" is not in the update. Strong framing, but it needs confirmation or softer wording.
"Dating apps are selling AI to users who say AI ruins dating" pushes beyond the supplied fact. The update says some users criticized AI as inauthentic; "ruins dating" is sharper than the evidence.
The trend angle still needs outside category proof. B says that honestly, but keeping it as a full angle before sourcing comparable dating-app moves is a little generous.
